{{short description|Length scale at which eddy currents are significantly affected by viscosity}}

In [[fluid dynamics]], the '''Taylor microscale''', which is sometimes called the '''turbulence length scale''', is a [[length scale]] used to characterize a [[turbulence|turbulent]] fluid flow.<ref>Tennekes & Lumley (1972) pp. 65–68.</ref> This microscale is named after [[Geoffrey Ingram Taylor]]. The Taylor microscale is the intermediate length scale at which fluid [[viscosity]] significantly affects the dynamics of turbulent [[eddy (fluid dynamics)|eddies]] in the flow. This length scale is traditionally applied to turbulent flow which can be characterized by a [[Andrey Kolmogorov|Kolmogorov]] spectrum of velocity fluctuations. In such a flow, length scales which are larger than the Taylor microscale are not strongly affected by viscosity. These larger length scales in the flow are generally referred to as the [[inertial range]].  Below the Taylor microscale the turbulent motions are subject to strong viscous forces and [[Turbulence kinetic energy|kinetic energy]] is [[dissipation|dissipated]] into heat.  These shorter length scale motions are generally termed the [[dissipation range]].

Calculation of the Taylor microscale is not entirely straightforward, requiring formation of certain flow correlation function(s),<ref>Landahl, M.T. & E. Mollo-Christensen.  '''Turbulence and Random Processes in Fluid Mechanics.'''  Cambridge, 2ed, 1992.</ref> then expanding in a [[Taylor series]] and using the first non-zero term to characterize an [[Osculating curve|osculating parabola]]. The Taylor microscale is proportional to <math> \text{Re}^{-1/2} </math>, while the [[Kolmogorov microscales|Kolmogorov microscale]] is proportional to <math> \text{Re}^{-3/4} </math>, where <math> \text{Re} </math> is the integral scale [[Reynolds number]]. A turbulence Reynolds number calculated based on the Taylor microscale <math>\lambda</math> is given by

:<math>
\text{Re}_\lambda = \frac{\langle \mathbf{v'} \rangle_{rms} \lambda}{\nu},
</math>

where <math>\langle \mathbf{v'} \rangle_{rms} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{ (v'_1)^2 + (v'_2)^2 + (v'_3)^2 }</math> is the [[root mean square]] of the velocity fluctuations.
The Taylor microscale is given as

:<math>
\lambda = \sqrt{15 \frac{\nu}{\epsilon}} \langle \mathbf{v'} \rangle_{rms},
</math>

where <math>\nu</math> is the [[kinematic viscosity]], and <math>\epsilon</math> is the rate of energy dissipation. A relation with [[turbulence kinetic energy]] <math>k</math> can be derived as

:<math>
\lambda \approx \sqrt{10 \nu \frac{k}{\epsilon}}.
</math>

The Taylor microscale gives a convenient estimation for the fluctuating strain rate field

:<math>
\left( \frac{\partial \langle \mathbf{v} '\rangle_{rms}}{\partial \mathbf{x} }\right)^2 = \frac{\langle \mathbf{v}' \rangle_{rms}^2}{\lambda^2}.
</math>

==Other relations==

The Taylor microscale falls in between the large-scale eddies and the small-scale eddies, which can be seen by calculating the ratios between <math>\lambda</math> and the Kolmogorov microscale <math>\eta</math>. Given the length scale of the larger eddies <math>l \propto \frac{k^{3/2}}{\epsilon}</math>, and the turbulence Reynolds number <math>\text{Re}_{l}</math> referred to these eddies, the following relations can be obtained:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Pope |first=Stephen |title=Turbulent Flows |publisher=Cambridge |year=2000 |isbn=9780521598866 |edition=1st |pages=200}}</ref>

:<math>
\frac{\lambda}{l} = \sqrt{10} \, \text{Re}_{l}^{-1/2}
</math>

:<math>
\frac{\eta}{l} = \text{Re}_{l}^{-3/4}
</math>

:<math>
\frac{\lambda}{\eta} = \sqrt{10} \, \text{Re}_{l}^{1/4}
</math>

:<math>
\lambda = \sqrt{10} \, \eta^{2/3} l^{1/3}
</math>
